Alex K: Hey — running into a weird issue with the Go client + HTTP/2. When I cancel the context for a streaming request the handler stops processing but the TCP connection stays alive and the server keeps sending until idle timeout. Happens only when H2 is negotiated. Anyone seen this?

Maya P: hmm, do you call req = req.WithContext(ctx) before client.Do?

Alex K: Yep, using Request.WithContext. Code snippet:```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
defer cancel()
req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", url, nil)
resp, err := httpClient.Do(req)
// resp can be streaming 
```
Context cancel definitely fires, but server stream keeps going on the wire.

Samir R: what's your transport configured as? net/http default Transport (which enables h2) or a custom x/net/http2.Transport?

Alex K: Using a custom transport to tweak pooling: &http.Transport{MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 100, IdleConnTimeout: 90*time.Second, TLSClientConfig: tlsConfig} (then http2 is enabled via http2.ConfigureTransport).

Maya P: ok. two common things: (1) make sure you call resp.Body.Close() when ctx cancels — with HTTP/2 the stream can be left open even if the request context is done. (2) set an overall client timeout if you want hard kill semantics: http.Client{Timeout: 15*time.Second} will close the whole request.

Samir R: to expand on Maya — net/http won't forcibly tear down the TCP conn just because a single stream is cancelled. For multiplexed h2, other streams may reuse the conn. So calling resp.Body.Close() on cancel is the usual pattern to signal the server. Example trick: attach a goroutine that closes Body when ctx.Done():```go
go func() { <-ctx.Done(); if resp != nil { resp.Body.Close() } }()
```

Alex K: that helps, thanks. But I saw that sometimes resp.Body.Close() blocks if server is writing a lot. Any tunables to make the transport more responsive?

Maya P: you can tweak IdleConnTimeout and TLS handshake timeouts on the http.Transport. Also MaxConnsPerHost can limit concurrent streams so a stalled stream doesn't starve new ones. If you need aggressive kill, client.Timeout or manually closing the underlying connection (via transport.CloseIdleConnections or a custom dialer that tracks net.Conn) are options.

Samir R: another approach is a context-aware reader wrapper so reads return when ctx cancelled. Example pattern: create an io.ReadCloser that wraps resp.Body and returns ctx.Err() on Read when ctx cancelled. That avoids blocking callers on Read while you wait for Close to propagate.

Alex K: good idea. Any known Go http2 bugs around context propagation? I vaguely remember something in older Go versions where cancel didn't interrupt Write/Read in certain states.

Samir R: there were edge cases in older runtime versions; if you can reproduce reliably include Go version in the issue. But generally behavior is as Maya said: context cancels the request but the underlying connection lifecycle is separate for multiplexing.

Alex K: noted. I'll try: set MaxConnsPerHost, ensure resp.Body.Close in a cancel goroutine, and add a context-aware reader. If that doesn't cut it I'll capture pcap and open an issue with Go version + minimal repro.

Maya P: sounds good. If you want I can sketch a small helper in the SDK that wraps streaming responses and wires cancel -> Close. Could be a one-liner helper for users.

Alex K: please! that'd save time. I'll open a short PR and tag you. Thanks 🙂

Alex K: FYI I'll post the PR link once CI passes.
